title: Numbers, time, and days
goal: Count, tell the time, name the days and months, and place events in the past and future.
bekal: Sundanese numbers, including the ones that differ from Indonesian: *hiji*, *salapan*, *dalapan*
telling the time with *tabuh*, and a way of dividing the day that may not match yours

dialogs.title: Paguneman — Making plans with Néng Sari
dialogs.intro: Rani and Sari are sitting on the porch. Sari offers to show Rani around Bandung, and they try to agree on a time.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.id: Hey, are you doing anything tomorrow?

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Hayu urang ka Lembang. Kuring nyaho tempat nu alus.
lines.id: Let's go to Lembang. I know a great place.
lines.literal: come-on we to Lembang. I know place which good.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Hayu waé. Tabuh sabaraha indit na?
lines.id: Sure, let's. What time are we leaving?

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Isuk-isuk waé, tabuh tujuh. Ulah beurang teuing, sok macét.
lines.id: Early, at seven. Not too late, the traffic gets bad.
lines.literal: morning-morning just, o'clock seven. don't midday too, tends jammed.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Tabuh tujuh téh isuk pisan nya. Balik na iraha?
lines.id: Seven is really early. When do we come back?
lines.literal: o'clock seven [téh] morning very [nya]. returning-the when?

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Soré, kira-kira tabuh opat. Ké urang dahar heula di ditu.
lines.id: In the afternoon, around four. We'll eat over there first.
lines.literal: afternoon, about o'clock four. later we eat first at over-there.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Roughly how much will it cost?

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Tilu puluh rébu bulak-balik mah. Kadaharan mah séjén deui.
lines.id: Thirty thousand there and back. Food is extra.
lines.literal: three ten thousand back-forth [mah]. food [mah] other again.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Sip. Poé naon ayeuna téh, Sabtu?
lines.id: Great. What day is it today — Saturday?

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Ayeuna Jumaah. Isukan Saptu, cocog keur ulin.
lines.id: Today's Friday. Tomorrow's Saturday — perfect for an outing.
lines.literal: now Friday. tomorrow Saturday, suitable for play.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Sok atuh. Kuring hudang tabuh genep, nya.
lines.id: OK then. I'll get up at six.
lines.literal: go-ahead atuh. I wake-up o'clock six, [nya].

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Ulah kabeurangan! Kuring mah tara ngadagoan lila.
lines.id: Don't oversleep! I never wait long.
lines.literal: don't overslept! I [mah] never wait long.

notes: **Tabuh** = o'clock. It is always used for clock time: *tabuh tujuh* (seven o'clock). The loma form is also *tabuh*, so there is nothing to choose. To ask: **tabuh sabaraha?** = what time is it?
**Isuk** = morning; **isuk-isuk** = early in the morning; **isukan** = tomorrow. ⚠️ All three share a root and are very easy to mix up. Remember: the one ending in *-an* jumps to the next day.

**Beurang** = midday, daytime. *Kabeurangan* = to oversleep (literally "caught by midday"). The pattern *ka-…-an* here means "affected by, without meaning to" — the same pattern as *kahujanan* (caught in the rain), *katinggaleun* (left behind).
**Tara** = never, in the sense of habit. It differs from **tacan** (not yet, but might). *Kuring tara ngadagoan* = I don't do waiting; *kuring tacan ka Lembang* = I haven't been to Lembang yet.
**Hayu** = come on, let's (loma); the lemes form is **mangga**. *Hayu urang…* = "let's…". Note that *urang* here means "we", not "person".
**Ké / engké** = later. The short form *ké* is very common in speech: *ké heula* = hang on, just a moment.

**Ongkos** (fare, cost) and **rébu** (thousand) are borrowed from Indonesian. The Sundanese form is *rébu*, not Indonesian *ribu* — the same kind of small sound shift you see in other loans: *jaman*, *lampu*, *korsi*.

grammars.title: Numbers and how to use them
body: Many Sundanese numbers look like their Indonesian cousins, but several of the first ten are quite different and simply have to be learned.
after: The prefix **sa-** means "one, a": *sapuluh* (ten), *saratus* (a hundred), *sarébu* (a thousand), *sajuta* (a million), *sapoé* (one day), *sataun* (one year), *sabulan* (one month). The pattern is everywhere and you can apply it yourself.
Ordinal numbers use **ka-**: *nu kahiji* (the first), *nu kadua* (the second), *nu katilu* (the third). To ask: **nu ka sabaraha?** = which number (in order)?

⚠️ Halves and quarters: **satengah** (half), **saparapat** (quarter). For clock time, *tabuh tujuh satengah* means half past seven — the hour named is the one **already passed**, just as in English. Indonesian does the opposite (*setengah delapan*, "half to eight", = 7:30), and because the two clash, many people in Bandung now use the Indonesian way: *satengah dalapan* = 7:30. Follow the person you're talking to, and double-check times that matter.

blocks.text: To say when something happens, these are the time words you'll use most:

blocks.title: Telling the time
items: **Tabuh sabaraha ayeuna?** — What time is it now?
**Tabuh salapan leuwih sapuluh menit.** — Ten past nine.
**Tabuh dalapan kurang lima.** — Five to eight.
**Tabuh tujuh isuk-isuk.** — Seven in the morning. (add the time of day to be clear)
**Tabuh dua beurang.** — Two in the afternoon.

blocks.text: Month names are borrowed, with small sound changes: *Januari, Pébruari, Maret, April, Méi, Juni, Juli, Agustus, Séptémber, Oktober, Nopémber, Désémber*. Notice *Pébruari* and *Nopémber* — *f* and *v* become *p*, the habit you met in Unit 2.

Longer units of time: **poé** (day), **minggu** (week), **bulan** (month), **taun** (year), **windu** (eight years), **abad** (century). To ask the date: **Ping sabaraha ayeuna?** (what's the date today?) — *ping* is the Sundanese word for a date, although many people simply say *tanggal*.

blocks.title: Common time sentences
items: **Iraha badé mulih?** — When are you going home?
**Poé naon ayeuna?** — What day is it today?
**Ping sabaraha ayeuna?** — What's the date today?
**Abdi di Bandung tos tilu bulan.** — I've been in Bandung for three months.
**Kuring can pernah ka Ciwidey.** — I've never been to Ciwidey.
**Sok ka dieu unggal Minggu.** — (I) often come here every Sunday. (*unggal* = every)
